## Conclusion: The evidence does not support the claim that ivermectin lowers COVID-19 mortality

Your stated view is not well supported by the strongest current evidence. While early, small, and often low-quality studies suggested a mortality benefit, the largest, most rigorous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) found no significant reduction in death or hospitalization from ivermectin.

**Key evidence:**

- The **TOGETHER trial** (Brazil, NEJM, 2022) — a large, well-designed, placebo-controlled adaptive platform trial in over 1,300 high-risk outpatients — found ivermectin did **not** reduce hospitalization, prolonged ER observation, or death compared with placebo (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9006771/). The New York Times' coverage of this trial summarized the same conclusion (https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/30/health/covid-ivermectin-hospitalization.html).

- A rigorous meta-analysis in *Clinical Infectious Diseases* pooling multiple RCTs similarly found no convincing mortality benefit once low-quality and high-risk-of-bias studies were excluded, concluding evidence "does not support" ivermectin's use for COVID-19 (https://academic.oup.com/cid/article/74/6/1022/6310839).

- Much of the early "positive" evidence rested heavily on the **Elgazzar study**, an Egyptian trial that reported dramatic mortality benefits. This study was retracted in 2021 after independent analysts found the underlying data appeared fabricated or plagiarized. Because this single study contributed a large share of the pooled data in several favorable meta-analyses, removing it eliminated most of the apparent mortality benefit (https://www.theguardian.com/science/2021/jul/16/huge-study-supporting-ivermectin-as-covid-treatment-withdrawn-over-ethical-concerns).

**Bottom line:** The best-quality, large RCTs (TOGETHER, ACTIV-6, and others) consistently show no meaningful reduction in death, and the strongest "positive" data came from a fraudulent study. Major health authorities (WHO, FDA, NIH) do not recommend ivermectin for COVID-19 outside clinical trials. The current weight of evidence favors "no" rather than "yes."
